av_event.line_text: Joanne: That's good to hear. What do you do, Alison? Are you working?
av_event.what: A teenage girl in school uniform walks into the kitchen behind Joanne, fills the kettle at the worktop and switches it on, then walks back out of frame. The kettle's rising hum is faintly audible on Joanne's microphone for the next few lines. Joanne doesn't turn round.

text:
A: Hiya, can you hear me? Oh, there you are.
B: Hello, yes. Sorry, I was just sorting my glasses out. I'm Alison.
A: I'm Joanne. I'm in Taunton. Where are you?
B: Chester-le-Street. It's near Durham. Bit of a way from you.
A: Just a bit! How was your last one? I had a lovely gentleman, Graham. He's a solicitor.
B: Oh, I've not had him yet. I had a young lad, Callum. He was nice enough, erm, a bit quiet. He sells trainers.
A: Callum! That's my son's name. He's twelve, mind, so the only thing he sells is excuses.
B: Oh, bless him. I've got a son and a daughter, but they're grown up. Our Laura's in Newcastle and our Danny's in Leeds.
A: Do you miss them? Sorry, that's a nosy question.
B: No, it's fine. Yes, I do. Especially Danny. You worry, don't you, even when they're grown.
A: Oh, you never stop, do you. Mine are fifteen and twelve, and Ellie's got her GCSE mocks coming up, and honestly I think I'm more stressed than she is. She's sort of, "Mum, it's fine." And I'm thinking, is it though?
B: That's exactly how our Laura was. And she did lovely in the end.
A: That's good to hear. What do you do, Alison? Are you working?
B: Erm, not at the moment. I was in a school office for years, a primary in Durham. Then it all got merged into a trust and it was all screens and targets, so I left. I don't know if that was the right thing, really. I might do something part-time.
A: Oh, I hate targets. I'm a team leader at a call centre, insurance, and the targets are the worst bit. My lot are lovely, but you can see them panicking about their call times, and I'm like, just help the person, you know?
B: Yes. That's it, isn't it. I used to get the parents ringing up in a state, and you can't rush them.
A: No. You can't. You were probably brilliant at it.
B: Oh, I don't know about that. I just knew where everything was.
A: That's the most important person in any office, though! So what do you do with yourself now?
B: Erm, I walk a lot, and I bake for the chapel. Coffee mornings, that sort of thing. I do a lemon drizzle that people ask for. I'm not saying it's anything special.
A: It sounds special! I can't bake to save my life. My thing's a cream tea. Jam first, and I will fight anyone on that.
B: Jam first? I've never really thought about it. I just put it on.
A: See, that's very diplomatic, that is.
B: We go to Northumberland in the caravan every summer, near Beadnell. Do you go away?
A: Yeah! Static caravan in Cornwall, same week every year. The kids think it's boring, but they'd be gutted if we didn't go.
B: Oh, ours were the same. Steve still talks about the year it rained the whole week and we played cards for five days.
